778.title: Where is thy sting?
778.hook: Paul: O death, where is thy sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)
778.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals and at Easter, and the words "O death, where is thy sting?" are read aloud or sung in services about the resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Martha, who met Jesus on the road and heard, I am the resurrection and the life. Your line was christians hope this.

A letter is being read aloud to the church in Corinth. The writer is Paul, and he has heard something troubling: some there say there's no rising from the dead at all. His question is blunt: "how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?" A long, careful argument follows. Then, near the end, it stops sounding like an argument. Paul turns from the people in the room and speaks straight to death, the way you'd speak to a bully who has finally been cornered.
screen: `A LETTER TO CORINTH.` → `SOME SAY NO ONE RISES.` → `PAUL TURNS AND SPEAKS TO DEATH.`

segments.voice: Paul doesn't pretend death is gentle or natural or fine. He calls it by its name: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Whatever comfort comes next doesn't start by shrinking the loss. To explain how the dead could rise, he reaches for a farmer's picture: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." A seed goes into the ground, and what comes up looks nothing like the seed. "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." The body that rises, in Paul's telling, is changed, not just restarted. When that change comes, he says, "then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory." Some readers trace that saying to the prophets Isaiah and Hosea. Then the taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" It's almost playful, a little mocking, the tone of someone sure of how the story ends. And he names the sting: "The sting of death is sin," and then, "thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." For Christians, the line doesn't deny that people die or that grief hurts; Paul has just called death an enemy. It's a claim about who wins in the end: a sting and a victory, both asked after as if they had gone missing.
screen: `DEATH IS CALLED AN ENEMY.` · `A SEED SOWN, A BODY RAISED.` · `SWALLOWED UP IN VICTORY.` · `THE STING, NAMED.` · then, large: `WHERE IS THY STING?`

segments.voice: Let the line go by with your breath, one piece on each out-breath: O death, where is thy sting, O grave, where is thy victory. Then notice what comes, defiance, doubt, comfort or nothing at all, without deciding what it should be. If you pray, you can let Paul's thanks follow the questions.
Paul, who taunts death in his letter to the Corinthians, claiming death is swallowed up in victory and will not win in the end. Today's word.
Your line: swallowed up in victory. For Paul, the enemy is real, and it loses. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.

779.title: Sister Death
779.hook: Francis, near the end of his life, adds a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising Sister Death
779.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians sing or pray the Canticle of the Creatures, and in Franciscan communities the death of a brother or sister is sometimes spoken of as the coming of Sister Death.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paul, who taunted death: O death, where is thy sting? Your line was swallowed up in victory. Paul called death an enemy. Today, a saint calls it family.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. Mother Earth. These are the names in a song by Francis of Assisi, written in the everyday Italian of his region rather than in church Latin. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, or the Canticle of the Sun, and it praises God for each of them, as if the whole world were a household. Tradition says that near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, Francis added one more name to the family.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` → `A SONG OF THE WHOLE HOUSEHOLD.` → `ONE MORE NAME, NEAR THE END.`

segments.voice: Francis doesn't praise the sun as a lamp or water as a resource. He gives each a place at the table. Sister Water is useful and humble and precious and pure. Brother Fire is beautiful and strong. Everything in the song is kin. The new verse praises God for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living person can escape. Francis doesn't say death is pleasant, or optional, or not real. He says it is certain, and then he calls it sister, the same word he used for the moon. It isn't sentimental, either. The verse warns: woe to those who die in mortal sin. And it calls blessed those whom death finds doing God's holy will, for the second death will do them no harm. Some readers hear in that phrase an echo of the book of Revelation. For Francis, a sister can still be serious. An enemy is something you fight. A sister comes whether you are ready or not, but she belongs to the household. Paul called death the last enemy; Francis calls it sister. Both words come from Christian voices. Death is the same in both. What changes is where it sits: outside the door, or at the table.
screen: `EVERY CREATURE IS KIN.` · `OUR SISTER BODILY DEATH.` · `SERIOUS, NOT SENTIMENTAL.` · `AN ENEMY, OR A SISTER.` · then, large: `SISTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ending that has already happened, not a raw loss but a finished thing: a school year, a job, a move, a friendship that ran its course, a habit you finally put down. Look at what it made room for, and thank it, as if it had been a sister walking you to a door. If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God, as Francis did.
Sister Death: Francis of Assisi's name for bodily death in his Canticle of the Creatures, certain and unavoidable, and still counted as family. Today's word.
Your line: a place at the table. Francis gave even the last guest a family name. Go gently.

780.title: Dying well
780.hook: old Christian handbooks taught the art of dying well
780.howItsDone: Some Christians prepare for death with prayer, confession, anointing or last rites, and by talking with family and clergy; chaplains and hospice teams may help with what people call a good death.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sister Death, Francis's name for a death that is certain and still family. Your line was a place at the table.

Old woodcuts, in pairs. In the first, a man lies in bed, plainly near the end, and little devils crowd the room, whispering, holding up things to tempt him. In the next, an angel stands close with an answer, and the devils fall back. The pictures come from a kind of old Christian handbook, copied, printed and translated, with a two-word Latin title: ars moriendi, the art of dying. A whole book, written for ordinary people, about the one thing nobody gets to do twice.
screen: `A MAN IN BED, NEAR THE END.` → `DEVILS, THEN AN ANGEL.` → `A HANDBOOK FOR DYING.`

segments.voice: Calling it an art is the surprise. An art is something you learn, practice and get better at. The handbook treats a good death the same way: not as luck, but as something a person can prepare for while still well. It imagines the deathbed as a last struggle. The dying person is tempted to doubt their faith, to despair over everything they've done wrong, to grow impatient with pain, to feel proud of their own goodness, and to cling to their money, their things and their people. For each temptation, an angel in the pictures offers a counter. Against despair, trust in mercy. Against impatience, patience. Against pride, humility. Against clinging, letting go. It's less a list of rules than a set of turns the heart can make, even at the very end. The handbook also speaks to whoever sits at the bedside: questions to gently ask, prayers to read aloud, an image of the cross held where the dying person can see it. Dying well, in these books, was not meant to be done alone. And they carry a quiet suggestion: don't wait for the deathbed. The turns can be practiced now, on a day when nothing is wrong.
screen: `DYING AS AN ART YOU CAN LEARN.` · `TEMPTATIONS AT THE BEDSIDE.` · `AN ANSWER FOR EACH ONE.` · `NOT DONE ALONE.` · then, large: `DYING WELL.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself gently, without forcing an answer: what would dying well mean to me? Maybe it's who is there, what has been said or forgiven, or simply not being afraid; let one sentence form without polishing it, and if nothing comes, that's an answer too. If you pray, you can hold the question before God.
Ars moriendi: Latin for the art of dying, the name of old Christian handbooks that taught people how to prepare for a good death. Today's word.
Your line: against clinging, letting go. The old books called it an art because it can be learned. That's day seven hundred eighty.

781.title: All Souls' Day
781.hook: on 2 November, Catholics pray for the dead
781.howItsDone: On All Souls' Day Catholics attend Mass for the dead, write names in a parish book of remembrance, visit and tend graves, and light candles; Orthodox Christians keep their own days for praying for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ars moriendi, the old art of dying well. Your line was against clinging, letting go. Those books were about the hour of death. Today, what the living do afterward.

A Catholic church on the second of November. Near the door, in some parishes, a book lies open on a stand, and people stop on their way in to write in it. Not messages. Names. A mother. A brother. A friend from school. A baby who never came home from the hospital. Later, during Mass, those names are remembered and prayed for. In some towns, families are already at the cemetery with flowers and candles. The day has a long official name. The short one is All Souls' Day.
screen: `A BOOK OPEN BY THE DOOR.` → `NOT MESSAGES. NAMES.` → `CANDLES AT THE CEMETERY.`

segments.voice: The Church calendar calls it the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, and it comes right after All Saints' Day. All Saints honors the holy ones. All Souls prays for all the faithful departed, the ordinary dead, the ones people knew. Why pray for them? Catholics teach that some who die in God's friendship are still being made ready for heaven, a cleansing the Church calls purgatory, and that the prayers of the living can help them. The text Catholics point to is the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus and his men pray for fallen soldiers: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Orthodox Christians also pray for the dead, with their own days of remembrance through the year. Churches shaped by the Reformation generally don't teach purgatory, and their Bibles don't count Maccabees among the books of the Old Testament, though they remember the dead in their own services and prayers. Nobody needs to settle that today. Whatever the theology, the center of the day is a list. In parish churches, the old prayer asks for eternal rest and perpetual light for the dead. A person is remembered not as a number in a cemetery but by the name someone once called across a kitchen.
screen: `ALL THE FAITHFUL DEPARTED.` · `PRAYERS THAT HELP THE DEAD.` · `CHURCHES SEE IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE CENTER IS A LIST OF NAMES.` · then, large: `BY NAME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, family, a friend, a teacher, someone you knew only a little, and give their name one full breath, silently or aloud; if another name comes, give it a breath too. If no one you knew has died, choose a name you've read on a gravestone or a memorial. If you pray, you can use the old words asking eternal rest and perpetual light for them.
Purgatory, the cleansing Catholics teach some souls undergo before heaven, which prayers on All Souls' Day are believed to help. Today's word.
Your line: by name. Each name on the list carries a whole person with it. Until tomorrow.

782.title: Every soul shall taste death
782.hook: every soul will taste of death (Quran 3:185)
782.howItsDone: Muslims recite this verse in sermons and at funerals, and some families have it carved on gravestones; it is recalled when news of a death arrives, alongside the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was purgatory, and a book of names by a church door. Your line was by name. Today the voices turn to Islam, and a line about every soul.

A short line in Arabic: kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. In Pickthall's old English translation of the Quran, it reads: "Every soul will taste of death." It's short enough to carve on a stone or say at a graveside, and some Muslims do both. It sits in the third surah, the family of Imran, near a verse about being tested and holding on with patience. It doesn't argue. It doesn't comfort, not yet. It just says what is going to happen, to everyone.
screen: `A SHORT ARABIC LINE.` → `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.` → `IT SAYS WHAT WILL HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word kull means each, all, every one. There's no list of exceptions. Elsewhere the Quran tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that no human before him was given life forever. Every soul includes the strong and the weak, the famous and the forgotten, the one reading the verse aloud. Then the verb. The Quran could have said every soul will die. Instead it uses a word from the mouth: to taste. Some readers notice what that suggests: a taste is something you go through, and the one who tastes is still there afterward. The verse goes on: you will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is kept from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won. For Muslims, death is not a wall at the end of the road. It's a door, and past it lie accounting and mercy. The verse closes: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." In Muslim teaching this doesn't call the world worthless, since the Quran praises its good things too. It warns not to mistake the borrowed for the lasting. The same opening words come back in other surahs, and in surah twenty-nine they're followed at once by a return to God.
screen: `NO SOUL IS LEFT OFF THE LIST.` · `DEATH IS TASTED.` · `THEN THE DAY OF RESURRECTION.` · `THE BORROWED, NOT THE LASTING.` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL.`

segments.voice: Let the words come once, slowly: every soul will taste of death. Then, on each out-breath, let every soul be enough, every soul in this building, on this street, the people you love, the people you've never met, and you, held gently, as a fact and not a fear. If you pray, you can let the line sit inside your prayer.
The Garden, what the Quran promises to whoever is kept from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, after every soul tastes death. Today's word.
Your line: every soul. No one is left off the list. Day seven hundred eighty-two, complete.

783.title: An atom's weight
783.hook: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it (Quran 99:7–8)
783.howItsDone: Surah az-Zalzalah is short, and some Muslims recite it in daily prayer; Muslims recall its last two verses as a reason not to belittle small good deeds or small wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Garden, promised to whoever is kept from the Fire after every soul tastes death. Your line was every soul.

The ground moves. That's how the ninety-ninth surah of the Quran begins, the one called the Earthquake. The earth is shaken, and it throws up what it has been carrying. A person looks at it and asks: what is the matter with her? On that day, the surah says, the earth tells her news. People come out in scattered groups to be shown what they did. And it ends with two short, balanced lines: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of ill will see it.
screen: `THE GROUND MOVES.` → `THE EARTH TELLS ITS NEWS.` → `PEOPLE ARE SHOWN WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: In this surah, the ground itself is a witness. The floor you walked on, the street you crossed, has been listening, and on that day it tells what happened on it. Nothing done anywhere goes unrecorded. Pickthall's translation reads: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." The Arabic phrase is mithqala dharratin, the weight of a dharra, something tiny. Pickthall chose atom. Some readers picture a small ant, or a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam. Either way, it's the smallest thing you can still name. The two verses mirror each other. Small harms count: the sharp word, the little lie. Small goods count just as surely: the held door, the returned text. For Muslims, nothing is too small to be seen by God. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells a companion not to look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. So the great question of death and judgment is answered here in the smallest unit there is. Not a grand gesture. An atom's weight, done today, on ground that remembers.
screen: `THE GROUND IS A WITNESS.` · `THE WEIGHT OF SOMETHING TINY.` · `SMALL GOOD AND SMALL ILL BOTH COUNT.` · `DON'T BELITTLE A KIND FACE.` · then, large: `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go over the next few hours and find a small good waiting there, so small it would be easy to skip: a message to someone who's alone, a dish washed that isn't yours, a cheerful face for a tired cashier. Pick just one, keep it small, and picture it, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.

Your line: ground that remembers. Nothing done, good or ill, is too small to count. See you tomorrow.

784.title: The eyes weep
784.hook: when his small son Ibrahim died, the Prophet wept: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves (Sahih al-Bukhari)
784.howItsDone: Muslims point to this hadith to show that weeping over the dead is permitted and merciful, while wailing and words of protest against God's decree are discouraged; mourners are encouraged to say the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dharra, the Quran's atom's weight of good or ill. Your line was ground that remembers. The week ends with tears, and a father holding his son.

The house of a blacksmith named Abu Saif. His wife is nursing a little boy named Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. A companion named Anas remembers going there with the Prophet, who took the child, kissed him and breathed in his smell, the way parents do. Some time later they came again. This time Ibrahim was dying. And Anas remembers what happened next: the Prophet's eyes began to fill with tears.

segments.voice: The report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't start with doctrine. It starts with a father holding a child close enough to breathe him in. Before anything is said about death, we're shown love. A companion named Abdur Rahman ibn Awf is standing there, and he's surprised. He says something like: you too, O Messenger of God? As if a prophet should be above tears. The Prophet answers him: this is mercy. In this report, the tears aren't a lapse in faith. They're a sign of the mercy God puts in human hearts. Then comes the line the story is remembered for: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And to the child: O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting. Three parts of a person, each given its job. The eyes may weep. The heart may grieve. The tongue holds to what pleases God: no cursing fate, no wild words. For Muslims, patience in grief limits what is said, not whether tears fall. Look back over the week: Paul taunting death, Francis calling it sister, the old art of letting go, names in a book, every soul tasting death, a dharra of good. And now a father crying over his boy, and calling it mercy.
